guest.bio_context: Bryan Sapot is the CEO of Mingo Smart Factory and has spent 26+ years in software development and B2B systems. He previously owned a software consulting company that implemented ERP systems and has 18 years of experience in manufacturing. He wrote version one of the product (originally called SensorTracks) himself and is a network engineer and software developer by background.

context.transcript_excerpt: I'm Dan Langley and this is the Manufacturing IT Podcast. In each episode, I speak with key people of influence within smart manufacturing. In each conversation, we unpack and dissect all things Industry 4.0, from technology and trends to the ever-evolving digital manufacturing landscape. Let's get to it. Hi, everybody. Welcome to the latest episode of the Manufacturing IT Podcast. I'm joined today by Brian Savart, CEO of Mingo Smart Factory. Brian, welcome to the podcast. Hey, Dan. Thanks for having me. My pleasure, Brian, and good to have you on the show. I appreciate your time here. So maybe you can start, Brian, by giving everyone a bit of an intro into who you are and what you're doing at Mingo Smart Factory. Yeah, so I'm the CEO of Mingo Smart Factory, and what Mingo is is really a tool to do two primary things for manufacturing companies. One is help them manage the plant with real-time data. So being able to answer the simple questions of when am I going to finish this job, where is it at, and have that information more real-time at, you know, a manager or an operator's fingertips versus writing the things down on pieces of paper. The other thing that we really help people do is help with improvement projects. So let's say you find an area on a line or a machine that's really ripe for downtime reduction or quality improvements. We help give the data to the manufacturing engineers to really understand where the problems are, and then they can use that information to fix it, monitor it over time, make sure it's continually being improved, and then once they get the gains they want, they can sustain those over time. Yeah, it's a good intro, Brian. And so just to be for clarity, the platform is called Mingo, but the company is Mingo Smart Factory, right? It's the same. So the platform is Mingo Smart Factory. We just shorten it up just to make it easier. Yeah, no, that's cool. And Brian, look, you've had the business, I see, you know, eight, nine years or so. Talk us through your journey over that period because I know from being the founder and CEO myself, the business challenges, the iterations, the kind of complications. So talk us through your journey over the last eight, nine years with the company. Yeah, so what's interesting is where we are now is not where we started, and I think that's very common for most companies. So the idea for Mingo, and back then it was called SensorTracks. We had a goofy spelling just like most startups that no one could spell and few people could say, that's why we changed it. But anyway, it started when I saw a presentation by the CEO of Microsoft, Satya Nadella, and he was talking about monitoring like washing machines and laundromats and like wellheads in the middle of Texas where there might be a cow and a radio tower and no people. And I had thought this would be a really good opportunity to help mid-market machine manufacturers, like manufacturing equipment manufacturers, to be able to monitor their equipment in the field and then do that whole, like, software-enabled services model. So, you know, ship them spare parts before they need them and, you know, really understand when their machines are having problems. You know, nine years ago, we were way out ahead of that market, but the machine manufacturers to this day are still trying to build that, but they're not really ready. So we pivoted towards the end users and really monitoring the equipment in their factories so we can connect directly to the PLCs and use sensors and all kinds of cool technology to gather that data. And the product has really grown over time from a kind of a simple machine monitoring tool, like is it up, is it down, why, into this, like, comprehensive, you could almost call it a MES or a manufacturing execution system. pending_qa.q: How has a small software team remained lean while building a manufacturing platform?
pending_qa.r: The founders have 26-plus year careers in B2B software development, which allowed them to build version one themselves and make lean decisions about features. The company focused on inbound marketing rather than heavy sales and marketing staff, rode organic growth and referral networks for nine years, and avoided taking huge investment from private equity or VCs that would force them to chase sales at the expense of business value.

pending_qa.q: What is the cost of MES implementation failures in manufacturing environments?
pending_qa.r: Manufacturing companies are slow to adopt technology because failures carry high risk. If an implementation fails, the likelihood of doing another such project in that company is very low because the company consumes resources, diverts production engineering time, and impacts the bottom line. The failures are more costly in manufacturing than other industries, especially for companies running on thin margins.

pending_qa.q: What measurable inventory improvement resulted from moving from manual paper-based production tracking to automated data collection?
pending_qa.r: One case study with Ice Industries showed effectively zero inventory variance at the end of the year. When operators manually wrote down production totals on paper, they rounded to the expected numbers (e.g., always 1,000 parts per hour), leading to cumulative daily inaccuracies of hundreds of parts. Automated counting down to the stroke and individual part eliminated these discrepancies, improving financial covenants and loan calculations.

pending_qa.q: How much OEE improvement did a food manufacturing company achieve in the first year of implementing production monitoring software?
pending_qa.r: Louisiana Fish Fry increased their Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) by 12% in the first year. Based on their size and equipment type, this translated to approximately $400,000 a year in savings from increased production when machines were running instead of waiting for repairs.

pending_qa.q: What role does real-time performance visualization play in engaging manufacturing operators?
pending_qa.r: Scoreboards displayed on the factory floor show operators their performance with red, yellow, and green indicators against targets. This creates a culture focused on keeping performance green, aligns the entire plant, and engages operators because they understand what they need to do and can see the impact of their actions, leading to better morale and lower turnover.

pending_qa.q: How does providing data-driven feedback improve operator engagement and reduce workplace attrition?
pending_qa.r: When operators see that management is using data to understand their challenges and act on them, they feel heard and part of the team rather than just a cog in the machine. When supervisors see data showing an operator is struggling with a problem and actively work to fix it, the operator becomes more engaged and feels the company is trying to help, increasing job satisfaction and reducing turnover.
